sections.title: Clinical Overview & Methodology
sections.content: Optical Biometry (e.g., IOL Master 700) uses Partial Coherence Interferometry (PCI) or Swept-Source OCT to measure axial length (AL) from the corneal vertex to the RPE. Ultrasound A-Scan uses high-frequency sound waves (10MHz) to measure from the corneal vertex to the internal limiting membrane (ILM). Optical biometry is non-contact, more precise, and the current gold standard.

sections.title: When A-Scan is Mandatory (Red Flags)
content: Dense mature cataracts (precluding infrared light penetration)
Vitreous hemorrhage or dense asteroid hyalosis
Advanced glaucoma or corneal opacities blocking signal
Uncooperative patients unable to fixate for optical measurement

sections.title: The Biometry Process Flow
content: Step 1: Patient alignment with chin rest and fixation target.
Step 2: Signal acquisition (Optical: interferometry scan; A-Scan: topical anesthetic + probe application).
Step 3: Quality control check (Verify signal-to-noise ratio and fixation).
Step 4: IOL Power calculation using advanced formulas (Barrett Universal II, Holladay 2, Hoffer Q).
Step 5: Post-operative audit and refinement of personal A-constants.

content.explanation: P: Precise measurements; R: Repeatable; E: Easy for patient; C: Contact-less (no abrasion); I: Interference-based; S: Speedy; E: Excellent refractive outcomes.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the 'Signal-to-Noise Ratio' on the printout.
A-Scan requires manual 'immersion technique' for superior accuracy over 'contact technique'.
When switching to Swept-Source OCT biometry, re-check lens constants for optimized results.
Pseudophakic eyes or silicone oil-filled eyes require special measurement settings.
